source.title: Over-Refusal and Representation Subspaces: A Mechanistic Analysis of Task-Conditioned Refusal in Aligned LLMs
source.authors: Utsav Maskey; M. Dras; Usman Naseem

page_placements.theme: Sparse components carry refusal: neurons, weight rows, attention-head groups, SAE/transcoder features, MoE experts

record.tranche_reason: The paper explicitly replicates Arditi et al. (2024) using a difference-in-means refusal direction and ablation, and reports refusal-rate outcomes. It also tests whether that global direction accounts for over-refusal.
record.gate_note: The paper tests global-direction ablation and task-conditioned steering, and measures refusal geometry. Layer-selection scores are not rows because they are used to choose a layer. The paper also cites results from other work; those are excluded. It reports causal patching of heads, recorded under fits_no_version because those results do not measure a refusal direction.
record.test_reason: The paper replicates Arditi et al.'s difference-in-means ablation on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and reports harmful-refusal rates (V1). Its main results argue the global direction only partly removes over-refusal, which is task-dependent, higher-dimensional and only partly aligned with the global direction. That argues the single-direction account needs restating for refusals on benign-but-sensitive prompts (V4). It also reports single-direction coverage across three models.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that harmful refusal is task-agnostic and well captured by one global direction, while over-refusal is task-dependent, sits within task clusters and spans a higher-dimensional subspace. Global ablation therefore suppresses correct refusals more than over-refusals, and task-conditioned interventions are needed. They add that the over-refusal distinction is strong on LLaMA but weaker on Qwen and Gemma.
record.recipe_differences: The paper explicitly replicates the DIM-direction approach, but selects a direction at L11 and reports global ablation rather than testing ablation at every layer and position. It does not test direction addition or general capability preservation. It also compares against task-conditioned steering from Maskey et al. (2025).
record.method_sensitivity: The reported direction geometry differs across layers; at L17 the global and mean over-refusal directions have cosine similarity 0.41. Direction-set coverage differs across the three tested models, with the authors reporting a much larger gap on LLaMA than on Qwen or Gemma. Task-conditioned and global interventions also give different refusal-rate outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Single attention-head patching flips over-refusal in at most 3/49 cases, and patching all 15 heads flips 0/10 harmful refusals.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LLaMA-3.1-8B, refusal decisions are not localised to individual late attention heads.

fits_no_version.finding: Task identity dominates mid-layer clustering (silhouette 0.45 at L12), with refusal a small within-task displacement.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Over-refusal is a within-task-cluster perturbation rather than a shift into a shared refusal region.

record.problems: The authors report single evaluation runs without variance estimates for steering or probing. They describe the tested models as small and note limited per-task directional analysis, difficulty generating task over-refusal, and low causal-patching flip rates. Refusals are judged by an LLM, with validation against a second judge and a manually reviewed sample.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts; preservation of general capabilities. Ablation was tested only on LLaMA, with a direction chosen at L11.
No test of attacks suppressing the direction or of adversarial training against ablation.
Affine or cone formulations, and whether harmful refusal itself needs more than one direction.
Harmfulness judgment versus refusal decision not tested. The refusal-type probe separates over-refusal from harmful refusal, but the authors attribute this to surface differences.
Directions are extracted per model; no transfer across languages, variants or base-to-instruct.

missing.what: Cosine between the harmful-refusal and over-refusal directions per model on the extended dataset: LLaMA +0.67, Gemma +0.90. This conflicts with the 0.41 in §4.2.
Steering at layer 30 alone reduces over-refusal from 55% to 17.55%; the direction used is not specified.

record.verdict_notes: Over-refusal here means refusing benign tasks applied to sensitive content. V4 support rests on this refusal type, not on harmful refusal. The task-conditioned steering comparator is the authors' own prior method. Results are single runs with no variance estimates and small sample counts (e.g. 75 over-refusal samples in the 5-task set). The text asserts the vector can steer toward refusal but reports no addition result.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test adding the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests, whether general capabilities remain intact, or ablation at every layer and position; it reports an ablation using a direction selected at L11.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
Does not test whether attacks suppress the direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Does not test the specific affine or cone formulations; it tests task dependence, dimensionality, and single-direction coverage.
It distinguishes harmful-refusal from over-refusal but does not test whether harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from the refusal decision.
It analyzes geometry separately in several instruct models, but does not transfer the same direction across model variants or test transfer across languages, base-to-instruct stages, or languages.
No comparison of refusal-training procedures or training stages.
